summary: An IAB statement that the public DNS is a hierarchical name space derived from a single, globally unique root. It argues that the DNS cannot technically support more than one public root, which must be served by coordinated root servers under a unique naming authority. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: The Internet's phone book starts from one single first page. If there were different first pages, the same name could lead to different places, so there must be only one.

questions: can there be multiple dns roots
what is the dns root zone
what does the iab say about the dns root
subtitle: Why the public DNS can have only one root, and what that means for anyone proposing alternatives.

tldr.problem: Proposals keep appearing to run more than one public DNS root, which would let the same name mean different things to different users.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB argues from the design of the DNS: names must be globally unique, every domain needs a single maintainer, and root server addresses are hard to change because they are configured out of band.
tldr.outcome: The conclusion is that the public DNS must have one root, served by coordinated root servers under a unique naming authority. Private name spaces remain fine.

today: RFC 2826 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the IAB's position as of May 2000.

sections.title: The Core Claim
sections.content:
This is an Informational statement from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), not a standard. It says that a global network needs a globally unique public name space, and that the DNS name space is a hierarchy derived from a single, globally unique root. This is described as a technical constraint inherent in the design of the DNS.

It follows, the memo says, that it is not technically feasible to have more than one root in the public DNS. That one root must be supported by a set of coordinated root servers administered by a unique naming authority.

The practical risk: users of different ISPs who click the same link on a web page could end up at different destinations, against the will of the page designers.
sections.eli5: If two phone books gave different numbers for the same name, you could call the wrong person. So everyone must use the same first page.

sections.title: A Common Symbol Set
sections.content:
The memo starts from a general point about communication. Two parties need a common symbol set and a common interpretation of those symbols. For a public system this must be strengthened to a unique symbol set with a unique meaning, so that any party can start a communication that any other party can understand.

DNS names let people refer to network locations with a label other than a protocol address. They are meant to be globally unique: for one name at one time there must be a single set of records describing its addresses, resources and services. Applications on the Internet assume this, and users expect it.

Because the DNS is hierarchical, each sub-domain within a domain must have a unique meaning within that domain. To prevent conflicts, the DNS gives every domain, including the root, a single owner or maintainer. The memo calls this a technical requirement, not a policy choice.
sections.eli5: A name only works if everybody agrees what it means. Each part of the name tree has one keeper who makes sure no two things share a name.

sections.title: Coordination of Updates
sections.content:
The design and implementations of the DNS protocol assume that each domain has a single owner or maintainer, and that its resource records are changed in a single-copy serializable fashion. Even if uncooperating parties could somehow share one domain, the protocol gives a client no way to discover and choose between conflicting definitions. The client returns the first matching set of records it finds and assumes it is valid. The memo notes that this behaviour is embedded in the operating software of hundreds of millions of computer systems.

The memo also considers a future fix. Any such scheme would need objective rules agreed in advance. Its example: zone A.B could give authority Y all sub-domains with an odd number of characters and authority Z those with an even number. But then one set of rules has been agreed and a single unique space exists anyway. Some cooperation and agreed technical rules are needed, and for the root that means one generally agreed set of rules.
sections.eli5: If two people could both write in the same phone book without talking, a computer would just believe the first entry it found. To avoid that, they would have to agree on rules, and then it is one book again.

sections.title: Why the Root Zone Is Hard to Move
sections.content:
The root zone differs from every other zone in one technical way: the addresses of its name servers come mainly from out-of-band information. That information is often poorly maintained and, unlike other DNS data, has no automatic timeout. The memo says it is not uncommon for it to be years out of date at many sites.

A resolver with no valid root server addresses can never obtain the root's own name server records. A resolver with a mix of valid and stale addresses cannot tell which servers are the real ones when answers conflict, so it is hard to revoke a malicious root server or even route around a buggy one. In effect, every full-service resolver delegates the root of the public tree to the public root server or servers of its choice.

So changing the set of root addresses is much harder than changing any other delegation. The memo concludes that root zone management must be extremely conservative: updates kept infrequent and root servers closely coordinated. DNS Security Extensions (RFC 2535) help somewhat, but a similar out-of-band problem exists for the root zone's signature key, so tight coordination is still needed.
sections.eli5: Every computer is told where the first page of the phone book is, and that note is rarely updated. Moving the first page is hard because many computers still hold the old note.

sections.title: Private Name Spaces and Directories
sections.content:
The memo does not forbid private networks from running their own private name spaces. But if they want to use names that are uniquely defined for the global Internet, they must get that information from the global DNS hierarchy, and in particular from its coordinated root servers.

In its conclusion, the IAB admits the DNS may not suit every purpose, such as finding information when the user does not know the exact name. It expects directory systems to evolve to help with vague references, and expects their results to be unique DNS names that are then resolved normally, rather than directories replacing the DNS. It ends: there is no getting away from the unique root of the public DNS.

The memo says it introduces no new security issues and creates no new issues for IANA.
sections.eli5: You can keep a private phone book for your own house. But for names everyone shares, you must look in the one shared book.
